name: Data Quality for AI
title: Data Quality for AI
answer: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads, and it matters because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. The usual controls are tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts, which together describe what the data should look like and where it came from. For an AI system the stakes are higher than for a dashboard, because a bad row can be learned as a pattern and then repeated across many outputs. The scope therefore includes the tables, views and feature sets that feed training, retrieval and inference, not just the reports built on top of them.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Data quality work runs on the same SQL databases and warehouses that hold the data, with checks executed as queries against tables, views and materialized aggregates. Orchestration tools such as dbt and Great Expectations are common places to schedule those checks, and they write results back to tables that teams can query. Model Context Protocol servers are increasingly used to connect AI assistants to these systems, and this site currently tracks 2451 active MCP servers, 263 of them for SQL databases and warehouses. The site's own pages are built from a PostgreSQL database, which is a reminder that the quality of the publishing pipeline depends on the same kind of checks.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by writing assertions in SQL, such as checks for nulls, duplicates, out-of-range values, broken foreign keys and stale timestamps, then running them on a schedule or in a continuous integration pipeline. Teams profile new tables to learn their shape, define expected distributions, and set thresholds that separate normal variation from a real break. Lineage records show which downstream models and features depend on a given column, so a failure can be traced to its source and its blast radius understood. Data contracts turn those expectations into explicit agreements between the team that produces a table and the team that consumes it, and incidents are triaged with the same discipline as software bugs.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance for data quality rests on provenance, ownership and permission, because a team needs to know where a row came from, who is accountable for it and what it may be used for. Lineage and audit trails record the path from source system to model input, and data contracts document the agreed meaning of each field. Risks include privacy exposure when personal data is copied into training sets, regulatory exposure when data is used beyond its licence, and silent bias when a subset of the population is missing or mislabelled. Access controls, masking and retention rules are the usual ways teams limit those risks, and reviews check that the data's stated rights match its actual use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward treating data quality as a runtime property of AI systems rather than a one-time cleanup before a project starts. Expect more automated test generation, where a model proposes SQL checks from a table's profile and a human approves them, and more use of MCP servers to let assistants inspect and repair data pipelines directly. Data contracts are becoming a standard part of the interface between producers and consumers, and quality metrics are moving into the same dashboards that track model performance. The open questions are how to measure quality for unstructured and retrieved data, and how to keep checks fast enough for systems that read from a database on every request.
